author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: In a small California town in the 1950s, a restless young woman pushes against the limits of her life through a series of relationships — one of PKD's realist novels, unpublished in his lifetime.
page_summary:
Mary Anne Reynolds is young, sharp, and stifled by a small Northern California town. The novel follows her involvements — with an older record-store owner, a Black nightclub singer, and others — as she tries to force her way out of the narrow future the place has laid out for her, crossing lines of age and race that her community polices.

This is one of PKD's mainstream realist novels, drawing on his own years working at a Berkeley-area record store, and steeped in the classical-music culture he knew intimately. Like the other non-SF books, it went unpublished in his lifetime and appeared only after his death, in the 1980s. Its interest lies in the ordinary-world register of concerns that his science fiction would later abstract — authenticity, entrapment, the search for a real connection — handled here without any speculative apparatus, in a closely observed 1950s American setting.

biography_events.event: Phil works steadily at University Music on Telegraph Avenue in Berkeley, advising customers on classical recordings and absorbing the catalog knowledge that he will draw on throughout the fiction; he attends UC Berkeley briefly without completing a term.
biography_events.source: Sutin; Anne R. Dick (The Search, on the record-store milieu)
